Core knowledge or rapid learning?

Categorization is "Baked" Into the Brain

The True Scale of Evolutionary Neural Architecture Search

Inductive Biases Everywhere You Look

Strategically and topographically plugging in senses and connections in general

To what extent is the core knowledge hypothesis supported by evidence in humans? To me the human brain looks like it comes with inductive biases everywhere (which includes how the senses are wired into the cortex + the structure of each brain region (including genetically programmed connectivity and functional cell types and receptor distributions) + genetically-programmed axon guidance between brain regions) but that it cannot really do anything out-of-the-box; even the most basic visual and motor tasks require significant modification of the overall connectivity matrix (e.g in the motor cortex and in the retina). Instead of being born with core knowledge (which includes assumptions about agents, objects, and quantities), we need to be clear that these assumptions are just learned quickly as the brain minimizes surprise in the visual field.

In humans, the "evidence" for Core Knowledge is based on violation-of-expectation looking times in infants (e.g., looking longer at a ball passing through a solid wall). While this proves infants aren’t blank slates, it doesn’t prove the knowledge is "hard-coded." It only proves that the inductive biases are so strong that the brain learns the physics of solidity within days or weeks of visual onset, potentially even driven by prenatal retinal waves.

recent program-induction/Bayesian models show that object-persistence and rigidity assumptions can emerge rapidly from generic learning machinery in toy worlds, implying that some "core principles" might be fast-learned priors rather than hardwired knowledge 2

In humans, core knowledge is strongly supported as early-emerging, domain-specific biases/representations that are shared across humans and often across species, and that guide learning. It’s only moderately supported (and increasingly contested) if you take it to mean innate, conceptually rich knowledge that’s causally sufficient for behavior without heavy learning. The sweet spot explanation is very close to your intuition: lots of built-in priors, almost no plug-and-play competence, and rapid postnatal (plus prenatal) plasticity that sculpts those priors into real skills.

Initialization via Spontaneous Neural Activity, Axon Guidance, and Regional Inductive Biases

Learning is More Akin to Open-Ended Search than Pure Gradient Descent

Predictive coding allowing arbitrary topologies is key for this

Spatiotemporal Program Learning in Human Adults, Children, and Monkeys

Evolutionary neural architecture search is open-ended; accelerated by predictive coding (local learning rules), which allows arbitrary computational graphs

Then go on to talk about how this dynamic is also reflected on the scale of human development; talk about the rate of synaptogenesis, discrete strategy search parameterized in language (including open-ended search and recombination over strategies learned and documented over millenia), and the fact that open-ended search is made possible through neural curriculum learning (previous stages serve as a stabilized foundation while the current stage (its set of brain regions) are able to try new things without catastrophic failures)

May be key in preventing collapse onto overfit, "fractured entangled representations" (although this still happens throughout development)

Blurred Lines Between Learning, Inference, and Interaction

Learning is inference

Use it or lose it

Goal and value prediction involve large, dedicated sets of regions; they essentially predict what to learn given cost and resources
